meta_title: Integral of x/(√x+1) dx — NCERT Exemplar Q10 Solved
meta_desc: Solve ∫ x/(√x + 1) dx step by step with the substitution t = √x from NCERT Exemplar Class 12 Q10, plus a free 8-question integration quiz.

quiz.title: Substitution Integration Quiz: t = √x
quiz.intro: Eight questions on solving ∫ x/(√x + 1) dx by the substitution t = √x. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Exemplar Class 12 integration by substitution

questions.q: Which substitution best simplifies ∫ x/(√x + 1) dx?
questions.explanation: Setting t = √x removes the awkward root, since x = t² turns the whole integrand into a rational function of t.
Squaring t = √x gives x = t², which is what lets us replace every x in the integral.

questions.q: With t = √x, dx works out to:
questions.explanation: From x = t², differentiate: dx/dt = 2t, so dx = 2t dt.
The integrand x/(√x + 1) = t²/(t + 1), and dx = 2t dt, so the product is 2t³/(t + 1).
Since t³ = (t + 1)(t² − t + 1) − 1, we get t³/(t + 1) = t² − t + 1 − 1/(t + 1). Doubling gives 2t² − 2t + 2 − 2/(t + 1).
The integral of 1/(t + 1) is ln|t + 1|, so the factor of 2 gives 2 ln|t + 1| + C.

questions.q: Writing the result back in x, ∫ x/(√x + 1) dx equals:
questions.explanation: Integrating term by term gives (2/3)t³ − t² + 2t − 2 ln|t + 1| + C, then t = √x yields (2/3)x^(3/2) − x + 2√x − 2 ln(√x + 1) + C.

questions.q: Once the answer is found in t, the final step is to:
questions.explanation: Substitution is only finished when you undo it: back-substitute t = √x so the answer is in the original variable.

faq.q: Why substitute t = √x instead of t = √x + 1?
faq.a: Both work, but t = √x is the cleaner choice here because x = t² is easy to differentiate and it turns the whole integrand into a simple rational function of t that you can divide out.

faq.q: Why do we need polynomial division after substituting?
faq.a: The substitution leaves 2t³/(t + 1), where the numerator degree is higher than the denominator. Dividing first splits it into terms you can integrate directly, plus a 1/(t + 1) piece that gives a log.

faq.q: Where does the logarithm in the answer come from?
faq.a: After division, the leftover term is −2/(t + 1). Integrating 1/(t + 1) gives ln|t + 1|, which becomes 2 ln(√x + 1) once you put t = √x back in.

faq.q: How can I check the final answer is correct?
faq.a: Differentiate (2/3)x^(3/2) − x + 2√x − 2 ln(√x + 1). Simplifying the derivative brings you back to x/(√x + 1), which confirms the integral.
